title: Stock I: one transaction
note: Remember the cheapest price so far. Selling today earns arr[i] - minPrice.

title: Stock II: unlimited transactions
note: Every rise is profit. Book it and reset the minimum to today.

title: Stock III, version 1: memo
note: state 0 = free to buy, state 1 = holding. remk = transactions left. Each (i, remk, state) is computed once.

title: Stock III, version 2: table
note: Same dp as version 1, filled from the back. Rows are remk, columns are state. A cell reads the layer to its right in time (i+1).

title: Stock III, version 3: rolling arrays
note: dp[i] only reads dp[i+1], so two layers are enough. swap(after, before) makes today's layer tomorrow's.

title: Stock IV: at most k transactions
note: Version 3 with 2 replaced by k. The answer is the best after[remk][0].

title: Stock V: long or short, k trades
note: Three states: free, long (bought, will sell), short (sold first, will buy back). Ending in a short is a huge loss, so after[remk][2] starts at -1e11.

title: Stock with cooldown
note: Selling at i skips a day: it continues from dp[i+2], which is nextafter. That is why this one needs three layers.

title: Stock with a strategy (prefix sums)
note: Change one window of k days: first half hold (0), second half sell (1). Prefix sums make each window O(1).

title: Stock with transaction fee
note: Two states and two layers. The fee is paid on the buy.

title: Stock with cooldown and holding costs
note: rec(i) = buy at i and sell at some j (paying costs[j-i]), then jump to j + cooldown + 1, or skip i.

title: Stone Game I
note: Even number of piles: Alice can take all the odd-indexed or all the even-indexed ones, and one of those sums is bigger. She always wins.

title: Stone Game II
note: rec(i, m, turn) = Alice's total from pile i on. A player may take 1 to 2m piles; m becomes max(m, x).

title: Stone Game III
note: Take 1, 2 or 3 piles. Alice's best total is val; compare it with the rest (tot - val).

title: Stone Game IV: square numbers
note: rec(n) = can the player to move win? Yes if some square f*f leaves the opponent in a losing state: !rec(n - f*f).

title: Stone Game V: split the row
note: Split [i..j] at k. The larger side is thrown away and you score the smaller side. If they tie, try both.

title: Stone Game VI: a + b greedy
note: a-b karo, fir max nikalo. Taking a stone helps you by a and denies the other player b, so sort by a + b and alternate.

title: Stone Game VII: score difference
note: rec(l, r, turn) is Alice's lead. Removing a stone scores the sum of what is left. Alice maximises the lead, Bob minimises it.

title: Stone Game VIII: prefix + suffix best
note: A move takes a prefix, so only prefix sums matter. maxdp / mindp are running best values from the right, which removes the inner loop.

title: Jump Game: can I reach the end?
note: bandwidth is how far you can still go. Each cell may refill it. Stuck at 0 means no.

title: Jump Game II: fewest jumps
note: jitni baar paisa khatm hoga utne paisa chahiye. currpower is the current jump, maxpowergathered is the best next jump seen so far. When currpower runs out, take the next jump.

title: Jump Game III: reach a zero (DFS)
note: From i you can go to i - arr[i] or i + arr[i]. vis[] stops you from walking in circles.

title: Jump Game IV: same value teleports (0-1 BFS)
note: A value is its own node. Stepping onto a value costs 1, leaving it for any index with that value costs 0. So the deque pushes cost-0 moves to the front and cost-1 moves to the back.

title: Jump Game V: jump to lower, within d
note: Stacks first: pgeIdx / ngeIdx are the nearest taller bars on each side, which cap how far you can jump. Then rec(i) = 1 + best rec(j) over the allowed j.

title: Jump Game VI: sliding window max
note: dp[i] = arr[i] + best dp in the last k cells. The deque keeps dp values in decreasing order, so the front is always the window max.

title: Jump Game VII: binary string
note: dp[i] is true if some reachable j sits in [i-maxj, i-minj]. q counts how many reachable cells are inside that window: push when one enters, pop when one leaves.

title: Jump Game VIII: min cost
note: From i only two jumps ever matter: the next greater-or-equal (ngeIdx) and the next smaller (nseIdx). Two stacks find them, then it is a tiny memo.

title: Jump Game IX: max value reachable
note: pre[j] is the tallest value up to j. Walking back from the right, every index whose prefix max beats the running minimum shares the same answer.
